Question: What are the main sources of operational friction during service?
Shane Breslin — Response: The most common issue is not kitchen capacity but information gaps. During busy periods staff do not always know which tables have been seated which have active orders and which are waiting. That ambiguity slows down decision-making around seating and table turns.

Question: How does communication between front-of-house and the kitchen currently work?
Shane Breslin — Response: It is functional in quieter periods but becomes unreliable as covers increase. Verbal communication works when the same staff are covering the same sections but breaks down when cover changes or when multiple exceptions happen at the same time.

Question: How is allergen information currently communicated and recorded?
Shane Breslin — Response: A verbal declaration from the customer to the server is passed on to the kitchen. That is not a reliable audit trail. There needs to be a formal record of allergen declarations and staff acknowledgements to protect both the customer and the business. Staff currently use free text on tickets so that allergy information is printed on the ticket when it goes to the kitchen but this depends entirely on the server remembering to add it and there is no way to verify it was done.

Question: What are your concerns about adopting a new system?
Shane Breslin — Response: Training time. Several staff members joined recently with no prior experience of digital ordering tools. Any new system needs to be learnable within a single shift.
